sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Data-structure choices define which operations are cheap and which guarantees the algorithm can use. Go slices, arrays, maps, linked nodes, stacks, and queues are not interchangeable labels.

List the operations the problem repeats—index, membership, append, front removal, ordered search, or key lookup—and select a representation that makes those operations correct and clear.

For example, a parser uses a slice stack for nested delimiters, a scheduler uses FIFO queue order, and a frequency counter uses a map because each value needs a count.

Complexity is only one requirement. Mutation, concurrency, stable order, Unicode, memory layout, and the need to preserve original indexes can decide the correct structure.

Choose from the actual access pattern and constraints. A small linear scan can be better than constructing an index, while repeated lookups over growing data often justify a map or sorted representation.

sections.title: The core model: core data-structure trade-offs in Go
sections.content:
core data-structure trade-offs in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

An array value has a fixed length that is part of its type and copying it copies its elements. A slice is a small descriptor over a backing array and can change length within capacity. Passing or copying a slice header can still share elements, which matters for mutation and append behaviour.

sections.title: core data-structure trade-offs in Go example
sections.content:
~~~go
a := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
s := a[:2] // slice shares a's backing array
s[0] = 9
~~~

sections.title: The practical decision: core data-structure trade-offs in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether core data-structure trade-offs in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

A stack exposes the newest item and naturally supports depth-first work, undo, and nested parsing. A queue exposes the oldest item and supports breadth-first work or arrival order. Both can use slices, but their removal ends and memory behaviour differ.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: core data-structure trade-offs in Go
sections.content:
Failures around core data-structure trade-offs in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

For one lookup, scanning a compact slice avoids map construction. For many lookups, the scan repeats linear work and a map can amortize its build cost. The break-even point depends on input size, key type, memory, and how many queries the program actually performs.

sections.title: The important trade-off: core data-structure trade-offs in Go
sections.content:
core data-structure trade-offs in Go and choosing by habit solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Linear search accepts unsorted data and is often simplest for one small scan. Binary search reduces lookup to O(log n) only when data or a predicate is monotonic. If sorting is performed solely for one query, its O(n log n) setup usually loses to O(n) scanning.

sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With core data-structure trade-offs in Go, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

A stable sort keeps the original relative order of items that compare equal; an unstable sort may rearrange them. Stability is observable when equal-key records carry other fields. It is required when original order or an earlier sort acts as a secondary key, not for interchangeable primitive values.
